newsitem.title: USA: NYMEX oil complex hits contract highs, ends strong.
newsitem.headline: NYMEX oil complex hits contract highs, ends strong.

text.p: All three legs of the NYMEX oil complex hit contract highs Monday with gasoline posting the sharpest gains after a recent string of maintenance-related output cuts was capped off by problems at a large BP America refinery.
November gasoline rose 2.71 cents to 66.34 cents a gallon but hit a contract high of 66.50 cents near session's end.
"There are all these (refinery) turnarounds going into effect. It was mostly locals buying," a trader said, adding gasoline's rally may not continue given the lack of influential fund participation.
Volume was much higher in heating oil, with November heat ending the day 2.06 cents higher at 76.49 cents a gallon after reaching a contract high of 76.65 cents a gallon.
"This could be just an aberration for gasoline. Fundamentally, heating oil is giving the market it's strength," a trader in New York said.

November crude was buoyed by the rally in refined product prices, ending 51 cents higher at $25.24 a barrel after rising to a contract high of $25.28. Market sources said there were problems with a catalytic cracker at BP America's 231,500 barrel a day refinery in Belle Chasse, Louisiana.
BP America officials were not immediately available to comment on the reported refinery problems.

Among the refineries under maintenance, Sun Oil has said it would proceed with planned maintenance at its large 175,000 barrel a day Marcus Hook, Pa., refinery from October 4. Sun will idle a crude distillation unit for 18 days and a catalytic cracker for 44 days.
Heating oil prices have risen more than 30 percent in the last three months on historically low inventories. Inventories are being drained further by exports to Europe where stocks are also low.
This past weekend's colder weather in the northeastern United States, the world's largest market for heating oil, stoked supply concerns, traders said.
Crude prices were supported by news that the Louisiana Offshore Oil Port remained shut to crude oil tankers due to Tropical Storm Josephine. It was expected to reopen for crude deliveries by midweek.

Josephine continued moving rapidly toward the northeastern coast of the Gulf of Mexico Monday, prompting forecasters to post hurricane and tropical storm warnings for much of the Florida coast, the National Hurricane Center said.
At 1400 EDT, the storm was 110 miles south-southwest of Apalachicola, Fla. and was packing maximum sustained winds of 70 miles per hour.
-- Harry Milling, New York Energy Desk, 212-859-1761
